intro: Every sport keeps two kinds of records. One kind lists scores and champions. The other kind lists who was allowed to enter, and who paid for the room. This unit reads the second kind. You will study entry rules that decide which bodies a league counts: nationality rules, age lines, weight classes, Paralympic sport classes and the long, contested history of the women's category.

You will also follow the government into the stadium. Public bonds built ballparks in Chicago and across the country, and companies bought the names on public walls. Eminent domain cleared land in Los Angeles and Brooklyn. Congress protected a football merger and chartered the body that runs American Olympic sport, and a 2018 court ruling let states legalize sports betting. After deadly crushes and attacks, governments also wrote rules for keeping crowds safe.

As you read, track three things for each rule: which body wrote it, in what year, and which court or law later changed it. You will be able to set two sides of a hard argument next to each other, using their own evidence, before you decide what you think.
bigQuestion: How do rule books, courts and governments decide who may play and who pays for the places where sport happens?

title: Bodies, Data, and the State

chapters.title: Classification, Sex, and Eligibility
chapters.bigQuestion: Who decides which bodies a league counts, and what happens when a person does not fit the box?

story.title: Three Forms on One Desk
story.kicker: Every blank on an entry form was written by someone, in some year, for some reason.
paragraphs: An entry form for a high school meet sits on a coach's desk. It asks for a name, a birth date, a school and a grade. Each blank works like a gate. A student who is too old, or who attends another school, cannot pass. In Illinois, the state's high school association has kept those gates since the start of the 1900s.

A second form comes from an international wheelchair race. It asks for a sport class, written as a letter and a number. A panel of trained classifiers gave the athlete that class. The first organized wheelchair games, held at an English hospital in 1948, used no such codes at all.

A third form, from an Olympic past, once asked women for a certificate. From 1968 until the late 1990s, the International Olympic Committee checked women's chromosomes before they could compete. Men were never checked. The paper proved that a woman had passed a test the committee itself designed.

Each box on these forms was written by an organization at a particular time. People in meeting rooms voted the boxes into rule books. Later, others argued about them and rewrote them. Some rewrites came from courts, some from scandals, and some from athletes who challenged the box they were given.
story.think: Which box on a sports entry form do you think has changed the most over time, and who changed it?

lessons.title: Changing the Flag
lessons.mainIdea: Athletes compete for a country under nationality rules, and each governing body decides when an athlete may switch.
reading: An Olympic athlete does not simply sign up. The athlete must hold the *nationality*, or legal membership, of the country whose team puts them forward. The Olympic Charter, the IOC's rule book, sets the terms in its rule on nationality. An athlete who has already competed for one country usually waits three years before competing for another, unless the bodies involved agree to shorten the wait.

Zola Budd grew up in South Africa, a country then barred from Olympic sport because of apartheid. In January 1984, at seventeen, she ran 5,000 meters faster than the women's world record. The time was never ratified, because South Africa was not a member of world athletics. That April, Britain granted her *citizenship* in about two weeks, through her British grandfather, and she ran for Britain at the Los Angeles Games that summer.

The speed of Budd's passport caused a public fight in Britain. Critics said a star had jumped a line that ordinary applicants waited in for months. Supporters said her grandfather gave her a real legal claim. Soccer has its own rule book on the question. FIFA, founded in 1904, usually ties a player to one *national team* after an official senior match, though in 2020 it eased the rule for some players who had played only a few such matches when young.

words.d: legal membership in a country, which decides which national team an athlete may join
the legal status of being a member of a country, with its rights and duties
the team chosen to represent a country in international competition

look.title: Two Routes to a New Flag
look.text: Route one: an athlete moves abroad as a child, grows up there and becomes a citizen as an adult. Route two: a star athlete from a barred country gains citizenship in about two weeks through a grandparent, months before an Olympic Games. Both hold real passports. Both meet the written rule.
look.prompt: Should a governing body treat these two routes the same way? What rule would you write, and why?

check.q: What does the Olympic Charter usually require before an athlete switches countries?
choices: a waiting period of three years after last competing for the first country
a vote of the athlete's teammates
check.why: The Charter's nationality rule usually asks for three years since the athlete last competed for the first country.

check.q: Why was Zola Budd's 1984 world-best time at 5,000 meters never ratified?
choices: She ran on a road, not a track.
South Africa was not a member of world athletics.
She was too young to race.
She ran for Britain that day.
check.why: South Africa was barred from world athletics because of apartheid, so her time could not count.

check.q: How did Zola Budd qualify for British citizenship in 1984?
choices: She had lived in London for ten years.
check.why: Her British grandfather gave her a legal claim, and citizenship came in about two weeks.

lessons.title: Age as a Line
lessons.mainIdea: Age limits in youth, Olympic and pro sport are written rules, and breaking one can erase a result.
reading: Little League Baseball began in Williamsport, Pennsylvania, in 1939. Its founder, Carl Stotz, set an *age limit* so that children would play against others of about the same size. The Little League World Series, first held in 1947, is for players no older than twelve under its rules at the time.

In 2001 a pitcher named Danny Almonte led a team from the Bronx, New York, to the World Series. Reporters then found records in the Dominican Republic showing he was fourteen. Little League ruled him ineligible and *vacated* the team's wins from that summer. Adults, not the player, had supplied the false birth date.

Professional leagues also draw age lines. After Red Grange signed with the Chicago Bears in 1925, days after his last game for the University of Illinois, the NFL adopted a rule against signing players before their college class graduated. In 2004 running back Maurice Clarett sued over the NFL's version of that rule. A federal appeals court upheld it because it was part of *collective bargaining* between the league and its players' union.

Gymnastics drew its own line. In 1997 the International Gymnastics Federation raised the minimum age for senior events, including the Olympics, to sixteen in the year of competition. One member of China's bronze-medal women's team at the 2000 Sydney Games was later found to have been fourteen. In 2010 the IOC took the team's bronze medal away and awarded it to the United States.

words.d: a rule setting the youngest or oldest age allowed to compete
officially erased, as when wins or titles are removed from the record
talks in which a union and employers agree on rules for pay and work

look.title: Two Age Lines
look.text: Line one: Little League says players in its World Series division may be no older than twelve, so that children of similar size play each other. Line two: world gymnastics says Olympic gymnasts must turn at least sixteen in the year of competition. Both lines were broken by false birth records, and both times a result was taken away years or weeks later.
look.prompt: Why might one body set a top age and another set a bottom age? What is each line trying to protect?

check.q: What happened to Danny Almonte's team in 2001?
choices: It was moved to an older division.
It won the World Series and kept the title.
It was invited back the next year.
Its wins were vacated after records showed he was fourteen.
check.why: Little League vacated the Bronx team's wins after birth records showed Almonte was fourteen.

check.q: Which player's signing with the Chicago Bears in 1925 led the NFL to adopt a rule about college players?
check.why: Red Grange signed with the Bears days after his last University of Illinois game, and the NFL then barred signing players before their class graduated.

check.q: What happened to China's 2000 Olympic women's gymnastics team bronze medal?
choices: It was given to Romania in 2000.
The IOC took it away in 2010 because one gymnast was underage.
It was shared with the United States.
check.why: The IOC found one gymnast had been fourteen and gave the bronze to the United States in 2010.

lessons.title: Weight Classes and a Hard Winter
lessons.mainIdea: Wrestling sorts bodies by weight, and three college deaths in 1997 forced new rules on how athletes make weight.
reading: In wrestling, a *weight class* groups athletes within a set range of body weight, so that people of similar size meet. Each athlete must pass a *weigh-in*, an official check on a scale, before competing. Modern Olympic wrestling has used weight classes since the early 1900s, and school and college wrestling in the United States adopted the same system.

Weight classes also create pressure to lose weight quickly before a weigh-in. In late 1997, three college wrestlers died within about six weeks while trying to drop weight fast. They wrestled for schools in North Carolina, Wisconsin and Michigan. Their deaths drew national attention and led to federal and medical studies of rapid weight loss in the sport.

The NCAA rewrote its rules for the 1998–99 season. It banned rubber suits, saunas and other ways of sweating off weight, and it moved weigh-ins closer to the start of competition. It also raised the limits of its weight classes. In the 2000s the national high school federation added a program that sets each wrestler's *minimum weight* for the season, based on a body-fat and hydration test.

words.d: a group of athletes within a set range of body weight who compete against each other
an official check of an athlete's weight on a scale before competing
the lowest weight a wrestler may compete at in a season, set by a health test

look.title: A Scale Before the Match
look.text: A weight class promises a fair match between people of similar size. But the scale reads only once, at the weigh-in. Before 1998, a college wrestler could lose several pounds in the hours before stepping on it, then regain them before competing. The new rules of 1998 moved the scale closer to the match and banned the fastest ways of shedding weight.
look.prompt: Why did moving the weigh-in closer to the match make the weight class mean more? What other rule might help?

check.q: What is a weigh-in?
choices: an official check of an athlete's weight before competing
check.why: A weigh-in confirms that a wrestler fits the weight class before competing.

check.q: What led the NCAA to rewrite its wrestling weight rules in 1998?
choices: the deaths of three college wrestlers in late 1997
check.why: Three college wrestlers died in late 1997 while trying to lose weight fast.

check.q: What does a minimum weight program set for each high school wrestler?
choices: the number of matches in a season
the lowest weight the wrestler may compete at that season
check.why: The program uses a body-fat and hydration test to set a lowest allowed weight for the season.

lessons.title: A Racer Sues Her School
lessons.mainIdea: In 2006 wheelchair racer Tatyana McFadden sued to race alongside her high school teammates, and Maryland then wrote a new law.
reading: Tatyana McFadden was born in Russia in 1989 with spina bifida, a condition of the spine that affects the legs. She spent her early years in an orphanage and was adopted by an American family, who brought her to Maryland. At fifteen she won a silver and a bronze medal in wheelchair racing at the 2004 Paralympic Games in Athens.

At Atholton High School in Howard County, Maryland, she joined the track team. School officials had her race in separate *heats*, alone on the track, and her results did not count toward team scores. In 2006 she and her mother sued the school system under federal disability law. A federal judge granted an *injunction*, an order that she be allowed to race on the track at the same time as the other runners.

The case did not end with one athlete. In 2008 Maryland passed the Fitness and Athletics Equity for Students with Disabilities Act. In its title, *equity* means fairness in giving each student a real chance. It required school systems to give students with disabilities fair chances to take part in physical education and school sports, including adapted and combined teams. McFadden went on to win many Paralympic gold medals and major marathon titles.

words.d: separate rounds of a race, each run by a smaller group of athletes
a court order that tells someone to do, or stop doing, a certain thing
fairness in giving people what they need to have an equal chance

look.title: Alone on the Track
look.text: Picture a school meet in 2006. The runners in one race line up together. A wheelchair racer from the same school waits for a separate start, crosses the finish alone and sees no points added to the team total. A judge's order and, two years later, a state law changed that picture in Maryland.
look.prompt: What changed for this athlete when she raced at the same time as her teammates, even if her event was scored in its own way?

check.q: Why did Tatyana McFadden sue her school system in 2006?
choices: to race at the same time as other runners and not alone
check.why: She had been made to race in separate heats, alone, with no points for her team.

check.q: What is an injunction?
choices: a court order to do or stop doing something
check.why: A judge's injunction ordered that McFadden be allowed to race with the other runners.

check.q: What did Maryland's 2008 law require of school systems?
choices: fair chances for students with disabilities in physical education and school sports
one state champion in each sport
check.why: The Fitness and Athletics Equity for Students with Disabilities Act required fair chances in PE and sports.

lessons.title: Arguing Over a Class
lessons.mainIdea: Paralympic sport draws lines for who is eligible and who shares a class, and athletes can challenge where those lines fall.
reading: Early disability sport grouped athletes by medical diagnosis, with separate classes for each group. That produced many events with only a few entrants each. From the late 1980s, many sports moved to *functional classification*. It asks how much an impairment limits the actions a sport needs, so athletes with different conditions can share one class.

Every sport also sets *minimum impairment criteria*, the least impairment an athlete must have to be eligible at all. The IPC recognizes ten eligible impairment types, including impaired muscle power, limb deficiency, vision impairment and intellectual impairment. Each sport draws its own line, so an athlete who is not eligible in one sport may still be eligible in another.

A class is not always final. Some athletes hold a class marked for review, often because they are young or their condition can change. Athletes and coaches may file protests. The IPC's rules also punish *intentional misrepresentation*, meaning an athlete pretending during testing to have more impairment than they really have.

Disputes are common. Athletes in several sports have said publicly that rivals were placed in classes where they faced people with more impairment. The IPC has answered by calling for evidence-based classification. That means funding research that measures, sport by sport, how each impairment affects performance.

words.d: grouping athletes by how an impairment affects the actions of a sport
the least impairment an athlete must have to be eligible in a sport
pretending during classification to have more impairment than one has

look.title: Two Swimmers, One Class
look.text: Two swimmers share a class. One has a condition that has stayed the same since birth. The other has a condition that has grown weaker over time, and her class is marked for review. After a race, a coach files a protest saying the class mixes athletes with very different limits.
look.prompt: What evidence should a classification panel look at before deciding the protest?

check.q: What are minimum impairment criteria?
choices: the fastest time allowed in a class
the least impairment an athlete must have to be eligible
the age limit for Paralympic sport
the number of events in a Games
check.why: Minimum impairment criteria set the eligibility line for each sport.

check.q: What does intentional misrepresentation mean in classification?
choices: pretending to have more impairment than one has
check.why: The IPC punishes athletes who pretend during testing to be more impaired than they are.

check.q: Why did many sports move to functional classification?
choices: to let only one impairment group compete
because many diagnosis-based classes had very few entrants
check.why: Grouping by effect on the sport let athletes with different conditions share classes.

lessons.title: Sydney 2000 and a Broken Class
lessons.mainIdea: A cheating scandal at the 2000 Paralympics led to intellectual impairment events being suspended for twelve years.
reading: Spain's basketball team won gold in the *intellectual impairment* event at the 2000 Paralympic Games in Sydney, Australia. A few weeks later, a Spanish journalist who had played on the team revealed the truth. Most of the players had no intellectual impairment at all. No one had checked their papers with care.

Spain's Paralympic committee returned the medals. The International Paralympic Committee then suspended every event for athletes with intellectual impairment. The suspension hurt thousands of honest athletes around the world who had done nothing wrong. It showed that a class is only as fair as the *verification* behind it.

Rebuilding took more than a decade. Sports bodies worked with researchers to design tests that measured how intellectual impairment affects a specific sport. Athletes now needed records showing that the impairment began before age eighteen. At the London 2012 Paralympics, athletes with intellectual impairment returned in three sports: athletics, swimming and table tennis.

words.d: a lasting difference in learning and reasoning that begins in childhood, one of the Paralympic impairment types
checking that the facts on a form or record are true
stopped for a time, with the chance of starting again later

look.title: One Team, Many Athletes
look.text: In 2000 a single team broke the rules of one class in one sport. The governing body answered by stopping every event in that class, in every sport, for twelve years. Honest swimmers and runners with intellectual impairment lost their Paralympic events along with the team that cheated.
look.prompt: Was a full suspension the best way to protect the class? What else could the governing body have done?

check.q: What happened after Spain's 2000 Paralympic basketball team was exposed?
choices: The team kept its gold medals.
The IPC moved the Games to London.
Spain was barred from all future Games.
The IPC suspended all intellectual impairment events.
check.why: The IPC stopped every intellectual impairment event after the Sydney scandal.

check.q: When did athletes with intellectual impairment return to the Paralympics?
check.why: They returned at London 2012 in athletics, swimming and table tennis.

check.q: What does verification mean on an entry form?
choices: checking that its facts are true
check.why: Verification is checking that the facts on a form or record are true.

lessons.title: A Golf Cart at the Supreme Court
lessons.mainIdea: In 2001 the Supreme Court ruled that disability law required the PGA Tour to let Casey Martin ride a cart.
reading: Casey Martin grew up in Oregon and played golf at Stanford University. He was born with Klippel-Trenaunay-Weber syndrome, a circulation disorder in his right leg. Walking a full course caused him pain and put his leg at serious risk. In 1997 he asked the PGA Tour to let him ride a cart in its events.

The Tour said walking was part of the test of skill at the top level and refused. Martin sued under the *Americans with Disabilities Act* of 1990. A federal court in Oregon ruled for him in 1998, and a federal appeals court agreed in 2000. The Tour then took the case to the U.S. Supreme Court.

In PGA Tour, Inc. v. Martin (2001), the Court ruled 7–2 that a cart was a *reasonable modification* the law required. Justice John Paul Stevens wrote that walking was not essential to golf itself. In a *dissent*, Justice Antonin Scalia argued that a sports body should make its own rules and that judges should not decide what is essential to a game.

The ruling also settled a split between courts. In 2000 a federal appeals court in Chicago had ruled for the U.S. Golf Association in a similar case brought by another golfer, Ford Olinger. After the Martin decision, the Supreme Court sent that case back to be looked at again.

words.d: a 1990 federal law that bars discrimination against people with disabilities in many public places and services
an adjustment the law requires so an athlete with a disability can play, unless it would alter the core of the game
a written opinion by a judge who disagrees with the court's decision

look.title: The Court on a Golf Cart
look.text: The Court held that walking was not an essential part of competitive golf itself. It found that letting Casey Martin use a cart would not change the basic nature of PGA Tour events, so the Americans with Disabilities Act required the Tour to allow it.
look.cite: PGA Tour, Inc. v. Martin, 532 U.S. 661 (2001), majority opinion by Justice John Paul Stevens
look.prompt: What question did the Court have to answer about golf before it could decide the case?

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in PGA Tour, Inc. v. Martin (2001)?
choices: The Tour had to let Martin use a cart.
Golf carts were banned from all tours.
Martin had to leave professional golf.
The ADA did not apply to any sport.
check.why: The Court ruled 7–2 that a cart was a reasonable modification the ADA required.

check.q: What did Justice Scalia argue in his dissent?
choices: A sports body should make its own rules without judges deciding what is essential.
Golf should be removed from the Olympics.
Every golfer should ride a cart.
check.why: Scalia argued that judges should not decide what is essential to a game.

check.q: What is a dissent?
choices: the main ruling of a court
a judge's written opinion disagreeing with the decision
check.why: A dissent is written by a judge who disagrees with the majority.

lessons.title: Blades Before the Court
lessons.mainIdea: Runners on prostheses have challenged track's governing body in a sports court, with different results in 2008 and 2020.
reading: Oscar Pistorius of South Africa had both legs amputated below the knee as a baby. He raced on carbon-fiber *prostheses*, often called blades. In January 2008 the International Association of Athletics Federations, now World Athletics, ruled that the blades gave him an advantage and barred him from able-bodied events. Its ruling relied on a study it had ordered from a German university.

Pistorius appealed to the *Court of Arbitration for Sport*, an international sports court the IOC set up in 1984. In May 2008 the court overturned the ban. It found that the evidence did not prove his blades gave him an overall advantage. At the 2012 London Olympics he ran the 400 meters and the 4 × 400 meter relay, the first double-leg amputee to run in Olympic track.

Later cases went differently. German long jumper Markus Rehm, who jumps on a prosthesis, won a German national title against non-disabled jumpers in 2014, but he was left off Germany's team for that summer's European Championships. American sprinter Blake Leeper challenged a World Athletics rule limiting the height of running blades. In 2020 the sports court upheld the height rule for Leeper, but it struck down the part that put the *burden of proof* on athletes to show they had no advantage.

words.d: artificial body parts, such as legs, that replace missing limbs
an international sports court, created by the IOC in 1984, that hears appeals from athletes and federations
the duty to prove a claim; whoever carries it loses if the evidence is unclear

look.title: Blades and the Sports Court
look.cite: Court of Arbitration for Sport awards; World Athletics records
look.prompt: How many years passed between the Pistorius ruling and the Leeper ruling?

check.q: What did the Court of Arbitration for Sport decide for Oscar Pistorius in May 2008?
choices: It moved him to a Paralympic class.
It overturned the ban on him racing in able-bodied events.
check.why: The court found the evidence did not prove an overall advantage and lifted the ban.

check.q: What part of the World Athletics rule did the sports court strike down in Leeper's 2020 case?
choices: the part putting the burden of proof on athletes
the whole rule on blade height
the rule on long jump boards
check.why: The court upheld the height limit but struck down the rule that athletes must prove they had no advantage.

check.q: What does burden of proof mean?
choices: the duty to prove a claim
check.why: Whoever carries the burden of proof must show the evidence for a claim.

lessons.title: Certificates and Chromosomes
lessons.mainIdea: From 1968 to the late 1990s the IOC screened every female Olympian's chromosomes, a practice many scientists criticized.
reading: Women first competed at the Olympic Games in Paris in 1900, in tennis and golf. Women's track and field events were added in Amsterdam in 1928. From the start, sports bodies kept women's events separate. By the 1960s, officials began asking how to decide who could enter the women's category.

At the 1966 European Championships in Budapest, officials required female athletes to undergo a physical inspection. In 1967 Polish sprinter Ewa Kłobukowska, an Olympic relay champion, was barred after a *chromosome* test. At the 1968 Winter Games in Grenoble and Summer Games in Mexico City, the IOC began screening women with a cheek-cell test. Those who passed received a certificate.

Geneticists warned that the test was flawed. Some women had chromosome patterns that differ from the typical pattern yet had no athletic advantage from them. Spanish hurdler María José Martínez-Patiño was ruled out after a test in 1985. She fought the ruling and was allowed to compete again in 1988.

The track federation ended *screening* of all women in the early 1990s. The IOC stopped universal *sex verification* before the Sydney Games of 2000. It kept the power to look at individual cases. That choice moved the debate from a single lab test to rules written case by case.

words.d: a thread-like structure in cells that carries genes
testing everyone in a group, not only people who raise a question
testing used by sports bodies to decide who may enter the women's category

look.title: Women's Category Milestones
look.cite: International Olympic Committee records; histories of Olympic sex testing
look.prompt: For about how many years did the IOC screen every female Olympian?

check.q: When did the IOC begin chromosome screening of women?
check.why: The IOC began screening women at the 1968 Grenoble and Mexico City Games.

check.q: What does screening mean?
check.why: Screening means testing everyone in a group rather than individual cases.

check.q: What did many geneticists say about the chromosome test?
choices: It was the best test ever made.
It should be used on men too.
It was flawed and ruled out some women unfairly.
It had no effect on anyone.
check.why: Geneticists warned the test flagged women whose chromosome patterns gave no athletic advantage.

lessons.title: Testosterone Before the Courts
lessons.mainIdea: Rules limiting testosterone in the women's category have been fought over by athletes, federations and courts since 2009.
reading: In 2009, eighteen-year-old Caster Semenya of South Africa won the 800 meters at the world championships in Berlin. The track federation, then called the IAAF, ordered her to undergo sex testing. Her private results were leaked to the press. She was kept out of races for about eleven months before being cleared in 2010.

In 2011 the IAAF adopted rules on *hyperandrogenism*, meaning naturally high levels of *testosterone*. Women above a set level had to lower it to compete. Indian sprinter Dutee Chand challenged the rules at the Court of Arbitration for Sport. In 2015 the court suspended them for two years and asked the federation to prove the advantage with evidence.

In 2018 the IAAF issued new rules for athletes with *differences of sex development*, or DSD. They covered races from 400 meters to the mile. In 2019 the sports court upheld them. It called them discriminatory but said they were necessary to protect fair competition. Swiss courts refused to overturn that ruling in 2020. In 2023 World Athletics widened the rules to every event.

Semenya took her case to the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled in her favor in 2023 and again, on narrower grounds, in 2025. The federation says the rules protect a fair female category. Critics include many doctors and human rights groups. They say the rules single out a small number of women, many from Africa and Asia. They also say the rules push these women toward medical treatment they did not ask for.

words.d: a hormone that affects muscle, bone and other body traits
naturally high levels of hormones such as testosterone
conditions in which a person's chromosomes, hormones or body develop in less typical ways; shortened to DSD

look.title: Two Arguments, One Rule
look.text: A federation argues: the women's category exists so that women can win, and high testosterone gives an edge in some events. An athlete argues: I was born this way, I have always lived as a woman, and the rule asks me to change my body to keep my job. The sports court in 2019 agreed the rule was discriminatory but still upheld it.
look.prompt: What evidence would each side need to show to win the argument? How did the 2019 court weigh the two?

check.q: What did the Court of Arbitration for Sport do in Dutee Chand's case in 2015?
choices: It upheld the rules at once.
It moved her to a men's event.
It suspended the rules and asked for proof of advantage.
check.why: In 2015 the court suspended the hyperandrogenism rules for two years and asked the IAAF for evidence.

check.q: What did the sports court say about the DSD rules in 2019?
choices: They were discriminatory but necessary for fair competition.
They were illegal and must end.
check.why: The 2019 ruling called the rules discriminatory but upheld them as necessary.

check.q: What does hyperandrogenism mean?
choices: naturally high levels of hormones such as testosterone
check.why: Hyperandrogenism means naturally high levels of androgen hormones such as testosterone.

lessons.title: Policies for the Female Category
lessons.mainIdea: Rules on transgender athletes in the female category have changed many times since 2004, and many bodies now write their own.
reading: Since 1975, federal Title IX rules have let U.S. schools keep separate boys' and girls' teams in many sports. That long-standing split is why the question of who may join the girls' or women's team carries so much weight. For decades the question drew little public debate. From the 2000s onward it reached sports federations, state lawmakers and courts.

The IOC first wrote rules for *transgender* athletes in 2004. That policy required surgery, legal recognition and two years of hormone therapy. In 2015 the IOC dropped the surgery rule and set a testosterone limit instead. At the 2021 Tokyo Games, New Zealand weightlifter Laurel Hubbard became the first openly transgender woman to compete in an individual Olympic event.

Late in 2021, the IOC issued a *framework* that stopped setting one rule for all sports and left eligibility to each international federation. In 2022 the swimming federation, now World Aquatics, barred transgender women who had gone through male puberty from its women's events. World Athletics adopted a similar rule in 2023. In 2025 World Athletics began requiring a one-time gene test for athletes entering women's events.

U.S. states have also written laws. Idaho passed the first state law limiting girls' and women's school teams by sex at birth in 2020, and many other states followed. In February 2025 a presidential executive order took the same position, and the NCAA changed its policy. Supporters of such rules speak of fairness and safety in the *female category*. Opponents speak of inclusion and the harm of shutting students out of school life.

words.d: the division of a sport set aside for women and girls
a set of guiding principles that bodies use when writing their own rules
describing a person whose gender identity differs from the sex recorded at birth

look.title: Who Writes the Line
look.text: In 2015 one body, the IOC, set a single testosterone limit for every Olympic sport. In 2021 the IOC handed that choice to each sport's international federation. Swimming wrote its rule in 2022 and track and field in 2023. Meanwhile, U.S. states and the federal government wrote their own rules for school teams.

check.why: The 2004 policy required surgery, legal recognition and two years of hormone therapy.

check.why: Idaho's 2020 law was the first of its kind, and many states followed.

choices: It grouped athletes only by country.

choices: It started chromosome tests for the first time.

choices: Each ended with a ruling that let an athlete with a disability compete.

chapters.title: The State in the Stadium
chapters.bigQuestion: When governments pay for, protect and supply sport, what do the public and the teams owe each other?

story.title: A Vote Before Midnight
story.kicker: A state legislature races the clock to keep a baseball team from leaving Chicago.
paragraphs: Springfield, Illinois, the night of June 30, 1988. Lawmakers in the state capitol face a deadline. If a stadium bill does not pass by midnight, the Chicago White Sox may move to St. Petersburg, Florida, where a domed stadium is being built. Governor James R. Thompson works the floor, asking members one by one for their votes.

The bill passes in the final minutes, and news reports later say the official clock was held short of midnight. The law gives new money to the Illinois Sports Facilities Authority, a public body created in 1987. The authority will sell bonds to build a new ballpark. A tax on Chicago hotel rooms will help pay those bonds back.

In 1991 the new Comiskey Park opens across 35th Street from the old one, which had stood since 1910. The old park is torn down. The spot where its home plate sat is marked in the new parking lot. The new park later takes other names, including U.S. Cellular Field and Guaranteed Rate Field.

The public authority owns the stadium. A privately owned club plays there and sells the tickets. Each night the lights come on over the field, paid for with borrowed public money that travelers in Chicago hotels help repay. The deal kept a team in the city, and it tied the state to a private business for decades.
story.think: Should a state borrow money to keep a private team in town? Who gains, and who pays?

lessons.title: Bonds Behind the Bleachers
lessons.mainIdea: Many U.S. stadiums are built with public bonds, even though economists have long found little proof that they grow local economies.
reading: Cities have built sports rooms for a long time. The Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum opened in 1923 as a public memorial to veterans of World War I. Chicago's South Park Commission opened Soldier Field in 1924. Cleveland Municipal Stadium, built by the city, opened in 1931. These early public stadiums hosted many kinds of events, not only one team.

Most new stadiums are financed by selling a *bond*, a public IOU that investors buy and the government repays over many years, with interest. Interest on many state and city bonds is *tax-exempt*, meaning lenders pay no federal income tax on it. Lenders therefore accept lower interest rates. In effect, taxpayers across the country share part of the cost of a local stadium.

In the Tax Reform Act of 1986, Congress tried to limit tax-exempt bonds for projects that mainly serve private businesses. The rule looked at how the debt would be repaid. Many cities kept using tax-exempt bonds by repaying them from general taxes instead of team rent. A wave of new publicly funded stadiums followed in the 1990s and 2000s.

Economists have studied this *public subsidy* for decades. In the 1997 book Sports, Jobs, and Taxes, editors Roger Noll and Andrew Zimbalist gathered studies of many stadium projects. They found no case where a new stadium clearly raised local economic growth. Supporters answer that teams bring civic pride and keep a city in the national news.

words.d: a public IOU that investors buy and a government repays over many years, with interest
free from a certain tax; lenders pay no federal income tax on interest from many public bonds
public money or tax breaks given to help a private business or project

look.title: What the Studies Found
look.text: Across the stadium projects the authors studied, they found no case in which a new facility produced a meaningful rise in local economic growth or jobs. They argued that most spending on games simply moved from other local entertainment, such as movies and restaurants.
look.cite: Roger G. Noll and Andrew Zimbalist, eds., Sports, Jobs, and Taxes (Brookings Institution, 1997)
look.prompt: If fans spend money at a new stadium, why might a city's total economy still not grow?

check.q: Why do lenders accept lower interest rates on many city bonds?
choices: The bonds are paid back in one day.
The interest is exempt from federal income tax.
The bonds are backed by team owners.
The bonds pay no interest at all.
check.why: Tax-exempt interest lets lenders keep more money, so they accept lower rates, and taxpayers nationwide share the cost.

check.q: What did the studies in Sports, Jobs, and Taxes (1997) find?
choices: Stadiums were paid only by fans.
No new stadium clearly raised local economic growth.
Cities made a profit on every stadium.
check.why: Noll and Zimbalist found no case where a stadium clearly raised local growth.

check.q: Which Chicago stadium did the South Park Commission open in 1924?
check.why: A public park board, the South Park Commission, paid for Soldier Field, which opened in 1924.

lessons.title: Chicago's Stadium Authority
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois created a public stadium authority that built one ballpark and rebuilt Soldier Field, while other Chicago venues were privately financed.
reading: The Illinois Sports Facilities Authority is a public *authority*, a body created by state law to do one job. The legislature created it in 1987. Its first project was the new Comiskey Park, opened in 1991. Its bonds are backed largely by a tax on Chicago *hotel rooms*, so many visitors help pay for the parks.

The authority later helped pay for a rebuilding of Soldier Field. Crews kept the old stone columns and set a new, modern seating bowl inside them. The stadium reopened in 2003 as the home of the Chicago Bears. The Chicago Park District still owns it. In 2006 the National Park Service removed Soldier Field's status as a National Historic *Landmark*, saying the rebuilding had changed it too much.

Not every Chicago venue used public money in the same way. Wrigley Field was built privately in 1914 and is owned by the Cubs. The United Center, opened in 1994 for the Bulls and Blackhawks, was paid for mainly by the two teams' owners. Comparing these buildings shows that each deal was a choice, not a rule of nature.

words.d: a public body created by law to carry out one job, such as building stadiums
the rooms whose rental is taxed in Chicago to repay the stadium authority's bonds
a National Historic Landmark, a place the federal government names as nationally important history

look.title: When Chicago's Big Venues Opened
look.cite: Chicago Park District; Chicago White Sox, Chicago Cubs and United Center histories
look.prompt: Which two venues opened closest together, and which of them used public bonds?

check.q: What pays back most of the Illinois Sports Facilities Authority's bonds?
choices: a tax on Chicago hotel rooms
check.why: The authority's bonds are backed largely by a Chicago hotel tax.

check.q: Why did Soldier Field lose its National Historic Landmark status in 2006?
choices: It was sold to the Bears.
The rebuilding had changed it too much.
It moved to a new site.
check.why: The National Park Service said the 2003 rebuilding changed the historic stadium too much.

check.q: Which Chicago venue was paid for mainly by its teams' owners?
check.why: The United Center, opened in 1994, was financed mainly by the owners of the Bulls and Blackhawks.

lessons.title: Selling the Name on the Wall
lessons.mainIdea: Since 1973, owners of stadiums, including public ones, have sold naming rights to companies, and some deals have gone badly wrong.
reading: Older stadiums usually carried the names of owners, cities or memorials. Chicago's lakefront stadium was named Soldier Field in 1925 to honor Americans who died in World War I. The Cubs' park took the name Wrigley Field in 1926, for team owner William Wrigley Jr. These names were chosen, not bought.

The right to put a company's name on a building, sold for a yearly fee, is called *naming rights*. One of the first big stadium deals came in 1973. Rich Products, a food company, agreed to pay $1.5 million over 25 years to name the new county-owned home of the Buffalo Bills. Rich Stadium kept that name until 1998.

When the building is public, the deal raises a question about who should collect the money. Terms are set in the team's *lease*, the contract that lets it use the public building. In 2003 the publicly owned Comiskey Park in Chicago became U.S. Cellular Field under a deal the White Sox made with a phone company. The park became Guaranteed Rate Field in 2016 and Rate Field in 2024.

A name can turn into a problem. Houston's new ballpark, owned by a public sports authority, opened in 2000 as Enron Field after the energy company agreed to pay about $100 million over 30 years. In 2001 Enron collapsed in fraud and *bankruptcy*. In 2002 the Astros paid to buy back the name, and the park was renamed for a juice company.

words.d: the right, sold for a fee, to put a company's name on a building or event
a contract that lets one party use another's property for a time, under set terms
a legal process for a person or company that cannot pay its debts

look.title: Names on Public Walls
look.text: Soldier Field, 1925: a name chosen to honor the war dead. Rich Stadium, 1973: a food company's name on a county building. Enron Field, 2000: a company's name bought back in 2002 after a fraud. Each is a public building. Each name tells a different story about who the building is for.
look.prompt: Should a public building carry a company's name? If so, who should receive the money?

check.q: What are naming rights?
choices: the right to choose a team's players
the right to take land for a stadium
the right, sold for a fee, to put a company's name on a building
the right to sell broadcast games
check.why: Naming rights are sold so a company's name appears on a stadium or event.

check.q: Why was Soldier Field given its name in 1925?
choices: It was named for a team owner.
It was named for a juice company.
To honor Americans who died in World War I.
check.why: The name honors Americans who died in World War I.

check.q: What happened to the name Enron Field?
choices: The Astros bought back the name in 2002 after Enron collapsed.
It became the name of Soldier Field.
It was chosen by public vote.
check.why: Enron collapsed in 2001, and the Astros paid to remove the name in 2002.

lessons.title: Moving Vans at Midnight
lessons.mainIdea: Teams that threaten to move gain leverage over cities, and some cities have tried to use the law to stop them.
reading: A *franchise* is the membership a league grants to one club, tied to one home market. Owners can sometimes move that right to a new city. The threat of moving gives owners *leverage*, the power to press a city for a new stadium. The White Sox deal of 1988 was one example of that pressure working.

In March 1984 the Maryland legislature moved to let the city of Baltimore seize the Colts football team through *eminent domain*. Before the law took effect, owner Robert Irsay had the team's gear loaded into moving vans overnight. The Colts left for Indianapolis, which had built the Hoosier Dome. Baltimore went without an NFL team for twelve years.

The city of Oakland, California, tried a similar move after the Raiders left for Los Angeles in 1982. The California Supreme Court ruled that year that a city could, in principle, take a team this way. Later courts blocked the attempt, finding that it would burden trade between states. The Raiders returned to Oakland in 1995 and left again for Las Vegas in 2020.

When the Cleveland Browns announced a move to Baltimore in 1995, the city of Cleveland sued. In a 1996 settlement, the team's name, colors and records stayed in Cleveland. The owner's players moved and became the Baltimore Ravens. A new Cleveland Browns team, in a new publicly funded stadium, began play in 1999.

words.d: the membership a league grants to one club, tied to one home market
power that lets one side press another to agree to its terms
the government's power to take private property for public use, with payment

look.title: Who Owns a Team's Name?
look.text: In 1984 the Colts left Baltimore and took their name with them. In 1996 the Browns' players left Cleveland, but the name, colors and records stayed behind by agreement. Cleveland got a new team with the old name three years later.
look.prompt: Why might a city care so much about keeping a name and a record book, even without the players?

check.q: What did Maryland's legislature try to do to the Colts in 1984?
choices: Build them a dome in Baltimore
Let Baltimore seize the team through eminent domain
check.why: Maryland moved to let the city take the team by eminent domain, and the owner moved the team overnight.

check.q: What is a franchise in sport?
choices: the membership a league grants to one club, tied to one home market
a stadium owned by a city
check.why: A franchise is the league-granted right to operate a team in a place.

check.q: What did Cleveland keep in the 1996 settlement with the Browns?
choices: the team's name, colors and records
check.why: The settlement kept the Browns' name, colors and records in Cleveland for a new team.

lessons.title: Chavez Ravine
lessons.mainIdea: Mexican American families in Chavez Ravine were pushed out for a public housing plan, and the land later became Dodger Stadium.
reading: Chavez Ravine is a set of hills near downtown Los Angeles. By the 1940s it held three close neighborhoods, Palo Verde, La Loma and Bishop. Most families there were Mexican American. Many owned their homes, kept gardens and animals, and sent children to a local school.

In 1950 the city's housing authority chose the ravine for a large public housing project. Residents were told to sell, and the government used eminent domain against those who refused. This *displacement* broke up the neighborhoods. Then, in 1953, the housing plan was canceled after a political fight over public housing, and the land sat mostly empty.

In 1957 the Brooklyn Dodgers agreed to move to Los Angeles. The city offered owner Walter O'Malley about 300 acres in Chavez Ravine. Opponents forced a public vote, a *referendum*, and in June 1958 voters narrowly approved the deal. In May 1959 sheriff's deputies carried the last holdouts, members of the Aréchiga family, from their home as television cameras filmed.

Dodger Stadium opened in April 1962. O'Malley paid to build it, while the public had supplied the land. For many Mexican American families in Los Angeles, the ballpark stands on a memory of loss. Historians, artists and former residents have kept that history alive in books, films and reunions.

words.d: forcing people to leave their homes or neighborhood
a public vote on a single law or decision
a public agency that builds and runs public housing

look.title: One Hillside, Three Plans
look.text: First plan: homes and gardens built by families over decades. Second plan: a public housing project, for which most families were bought out or forced out, then canceled. Third plan: a private ballpark on land the city supplied, approved by a close public vote.
look.prompt: At which step do you think the public's promise to the residents broke? Explain using the dates.

check.q: Why were most Chavez Ravine families first pushed out in the early 1950s?
choices: The city planned a public housing project there.
The Dodgers had already bought the land.
The land was made a national park.
check.why: The housing authority chose the ravine for public housing in 1950 and used eminent domain against holdouts.

check.q: What happened in the June 1958 referendum?
choices: Voters narrowly approved the Dodgers deal.
check.why: Los Angeles voters narrowly approved the contract giving Chavez Ravine land to the Dodgers.

check.q: What does displacement mean?
choices: moving a team to a new league
forcing people to leave their homes
check.why: Displacement means people are forced out of their homes or neighborhood.

lessons.title: Public Use After Kelo
lessons.mainIdea: The Fifth Amendment limits takings to public use, and a 2005 Supreme Court ruling let economic development count as public use.
reading: The Fifth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, ratified in 1791, says private property may be taken only for *public use* and with *just compensation*. Roads, schools and parks clearly count as public use. A stadium owned by a public body but used by a private team is harder to judge. Courts have had to decide how far the words stretch.

In Kelo v. City of New London (2005), the Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that a city could take homes for a private development plan meant to create jobs and taxes. Justice John Paul Stevens wrote for the majority. Justice Sandra Day O'Connor warned in dissent that almost any property could now be taken for a richer use. After the ruling, more than forty states passed laws narrowing eminent domain.

Stadium projects soon tested those limits. In Brooklyn, a New York state agency declared land near the Atlantic Avenue rail yards to be *blight*, meaning run-down property. It then used eminent domain for a project that included an arena. New York's highest court upheld the takings in 2009. The Barclays Center opened in 2012, and the Nets moved there from New Jersey.

words.d: the purpose the Constitution requires before government can take private property
fair payment the government must give when it takes private property
a legal finding that an area is run-down, often used to justify taking land

look.title: The Takings Clause
look.text: nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation.
look.cite: Constitution of the United States, Fifth Amendment (ratified 1791)
look.prompt: Does an arena for a private team meet the words public use? Argue one side using the clause.

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in Kelo v. City of New London (2005)?
choices: Only the federal government may take land.
Economic development can count as public use.
check.why: The 5–4 ruling let a city take homes for a private development plan meant to create jobs and taxes.

check.q: What does just compensation mean?
choices: fair payment for property the government takes
a fine paid by a team
check.why: The Fifth Amendment requires fair payment when private property is taken for public use.

check.q: What happened after the Kelo ruling?
choices: More than forty states passed laws narrowing eminent domain.
check.why: Many states responded to Kelo with laws limiting when land can be taken.

lessons.title: A Merger by Act of Congress
lessons.mainIdea: Congress approved the AFL-NFL merger in 1966 and, in the same law, gave the NFL office a tax exemption it later gave up.
reading: In 1959 Texas businessman Lamar Hunt and other owners formed the American Football League, which began play in 1960. The new league and the NFL soon bid against each other for college stars. In January 1965 the AFL's New York Jets signed Alabama quarterback Joe Namath to a record contract worth about $427,000. Rising salaries pushed owners in both leagues to look for peace.

In June 1966 the NFL and the rival American Football League agreed to a *merger*. Because it joined two competing businesses, the deal needed protection from *antitrust* law. Congress added that protection to a tax bill in October 1966. Two Louisiana leaders, Senator Russell Long and Representative Hale Boggs, helped pass it. On November 1, 1966, the NFL awarded New Orleans a new team, the Saints.

The same 1966 law changed the tax code. It added professional football leagues to a section for *trade associations*, groups that serve an industry rather than sell goods. The NFL league office could now be exempt from federal income tax. The teams themselves always paid taxes. Critics called the exemption a gift to a wealthy business, and in 2015 the NFL gave it up.

words.d: federal laws that forbid rival companies from teaming up to shut out competition or fix prices
the joining of two businesses or leagues into one
groups that serve the shared interests of an industry, often exempt from income tax

look.title: A Team for a Vote?
look.text: In October 1966 Congress approved the AFL-NFL merger, with help from Senator Russell Long and Representative Hale Boggs of Louisiana. Days later, on November 1, the NFL awarded New Orleans a franchise. Newspapers at the time linked the two events.
look.prompt: What would you need to find in the records to show whether the vote and the new team were connected?

check.q: Why did NFL and AFL owners seek a merger in 1966?
choices: Bidding wars for players were driving salaries up.
The AFL had run out of teams.
check.why: Contracts like Joe Namath's in 1965 pushed owners in both leagues toward peace.

check.q: Which city received a new NFL team soon after Congress approved the 1966 merger?
check.why: The NFL awarded New Orleans the Saints on November 1, 1966.

check.q: What happened to the NFL league office's tax exemption in 2015?
choices: It was extended to every team.
check.why: The NFL office dropped its tax-exempt status in 2015 after years of criticism.

lessons.title: A Charter, Not a Ministry
lessons.mainIdea: The United States runs Olympic sport through a federally chartered private body, and Congress tightened its oversight after an abuse scandal.
reading: Many countries pay for elite sport through government. Britain shows how fast public money can change results. At the 1996 Atlanta Games, British athletes won only one gold medal. In 1997 the government set up UK Sport, paid for largely by the *National Lottery*, which had begun in 1994. When London hosted the Games in 2012, Britain won 29 gold medals.

The United States took another path. The Amateur Sports Act of 1978 gave a federal *charter* to the U.S. Olympic Committee, making it the coordinating body for Olympic sport. It let each sport name one *national governing body*. The law ended years of fighting between the Amateur Athletic Union and the NCAA over who controlled athletes. In 1998 Congress renamed it the Ted Stevens Olympic and Amateur Sports Act.

The committee relies mainly on private money, such as sponsors and broadcast fees, rather than a yearly federal budget. That left Congress with little direct control. After former USA Gymnastics team doctor Larry Nassar was convicted of sexually abusing athletes, Congress acted. A 2017 law created a duty to report abuse and backed the U.S. Center for SafeSport.

The Empowering Olympic, Paralympic, and Amateur Athletes Act of 2020 went further. It gave Congress a path to remove the committee's board and to decertify a national governing body. It also required yearly funding for the Center for SafeSport. The state stepped in through law and *oversight*, not by running sport itself.

words.d: Britain's public lottery, begun in 1994, whose proceeds help fund sport and other good causes
a legal grant from a government that creates an organization and sets its powers
the organization recognized to run one sport in a country, such as USA Gymnastics
watching over and checking the work of an organization

look.title: Two Ways to Fund a Team
look.text: Britain: after one gold medal in 1996, the government created UK Sport in 1997 and sent lottery money to the sports most likely to win medals. United States: a private committee holds a federal charter, raises most of its own money from sponsors and broadcasters, and answers to Congress through the law that created it.
look.prompt: Which system gives the public more say over sport? Which gives athletes more protection? Explain.

check.q: What did the Amateur Sports Act of 1978 do?
choices: It gave the U.S. Olympic Committee a federal charter to coordinate Olympic sport.
It created a U.S. ministry of sport.
It ended the Olympics in the United States.
check.why: The act chartered the USOC and set up one national governing body per sport.

check.q: What did Britain create in 1997 after winning only one gold medal in 1996?
choices: UK Sport, funded largely by the National Lottery
a British Olympic charter from Congress
a single national team for all sports
check.why: UK Sport was set up in 1997 and funded largely by the National Lottery.

check.q: What power did the 2020 act give Congress?
choices: a path to remove the committee's board and decertify a governing body
to host the Olympics every year
check.why: The 2020 law gave Congress a path to dissolve the board and decertify national governing bodies.

lessons.title: The State Takes a Bet
lessons.mainIdea: A 2018 Supreme Court ruling let states legalize sports betting, and Illinois passed its own law in 2019.
reading: Betting on games is old, and so are laws against it. In 1961 Congress passed the Wire Act, aimed at bookmakers who took bets across state lines by telephone. In 1992 Congress passed the Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act, often called PASPA. It barred most states from authorizing sports betting, while letting Nevada keep the betting it already allowed.

New Jersey voters approved sports betting in 2011, and the state passed laws to allow it. The NCAA and the major pro leagues sued to stop New Jersey. In Murphy v. National Collegiate Athletic Association, decided on May 14, 2018, the Supreme Court struck down PASPA. Justice Samuel Alito wrote that Congress may not order state legislatures to keep a law on their books. This limit on federal power is called the *anti-commandeering* principle.

States moved quickly. Illinois passed its Sports Wagering Act in June 2019, as part of a large public building plan. The first legal bets in Illinois were taken in March 2020. The law lets large sports venues seek licenses to host a *sportsbook*, a place that takes bets on games. It also barred most bets on Illinois college teams.

The state taxes the money betting companies keep, and in 2024 Illinois raised that tax, with higher rates for the largest companies. Leagues that once sued to stop betting now sign sponsorship deals with betting companies. Groups that help people with gambling problems have raised concerns about young fans. Leagues have also added rules to protect the *integrity* of games from players betting on them.

words.d: the principle that Congress may not order states to pass or keep certain laws
a business or place that takes bets on sporting events
honesty; in sport, the promise that results are not fixed or bent by betting

lessons.title: From Campus to Draft
lessons.mainIdea: In the United States, schools and colleges train most future pro athletes, and leagues choose among them through a draft.
reading: In baseball, a *farm system* is a set of minor-league teams that train players for a major-league club. Branch Rickey built one for the St. Louis Cardinals in the 1920s and 1930s, and the club paid for it. In most countries, soccer clubs run their own youth *academies* in the same spirit. FC Barcelona opened its La Masia residence for young players in 1979.

American football and basketball grew another way. Public high schools and colleges trained the players, and pro leagues chose from them. Schools and colleges, not pro clubs, carry most of the cost of that early training. The public pays for it through school budgets, state university funding and tax breaks for donors.

Pro leagues set up the *draft* to choose among those players. The NFL drafted only college players at first, and today it still requires players to be three years out of high school. Major League Baseball's first draft, in 1965, made Arizona State outfielder Rick Monday the first pick. Baseball's draft includes high school seniors as well as college players.

words.d: a set of minor-league teams that train players for a major-league club
youth training programs run by pro clubs, common in soccer around the world
a yearly selection in which each club, in a set order, claims the rights to new players

lessons.title: Fences, Seats and Security
lessons.mainIdea: Disasters and attacks have led governments to write rules for how stadium crowds are held and protected.
reading: On 15 April 1989, a crush in fenced standing pens at Hillsborough, a stadium in Sheffield, England, led to the deaths of 97 Liverpool supporters. It happened at an FA Cup semifinal between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest. High fences, built to keep fans off the field, stopped people from escaping the crush. It remains the deadliest disaster in British sport.

The government asked Lord Justice Peter Taylor to investigate. His final report, issued in January 1990, blamed failures of police *crowd control*, not the fans. It called for top English grounds to become *all-seater*, with no standing terraces. Law and league rules followed, and top-division grounds became all-seater during the 1990s. In 2016 an *inquest* jury found that the victims had been unlawfully killed.

In the United States, the attacks of September 11, 2001, changed how governments see big games. The federal government began rating major events by risk, and the Super Bowl has been treated as one of the highest-risk events. In 2013 the NFL adopted a clear bag policy for fans. Security plans now join team staff, city police and federal agencies in one command.

words.d: the planning and policing that keeps a large crowd safe as it moves and gathers
a stadium where every spectator has a seat and no one stands on terraces
a court hearing, common in England, that finds out how and why a person died
